phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar stop [k] — Welsh c is always hard — with short open [ɛ] and trilled [r]; the light, unstressed first syllable.
Short close [ɪ] under stress with a voiced dental [d]; Welsh words stress the penultimate syllable, so the weight of the name lands here.
Labial-velar [w] plus open-mid [ɛ] and alveolar [n]; the unstressed ultima closes quietly.

pronunciation.approximation: 'keh-RID-wen' — every c is hard, the r is rolled, and the stress falls on the middle syllable, the Welsh penult.

kin.label: Medieval Welsh verse
kin.form: Kerritwen, Kyrridven — the early spellings preserved in the poetry that names her

kin.label: Ifor Williams (reconstruction)
kin.form: Cyridfen, 'crooked woman' — the original form the greatest editor of Welsh poetry proposed; the lexicon's gloss follows it

kin.label: Traditional analysis
kin.form: cerdd 'song, craft, poetry' + gwen 'white, fair, blessed' — 'fair of song, blessed of poetry', the romantic reading

kin.label: Modern Welsh
kin.form: Ceridwen, the unbroken living form — and the name of the awen's keeper

pronunciation.note: Ceridwen is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The etymology is a genuine scholarly debate: Ifor Williams derived the name from an original Cyridfen, 'crooked woman', while the traditional analysis reads cerdd 'poetry' + gwen 'fair, blessed'; the handbooks register both rather than settle the question.

domains.title: Inspiration, Transformation
domains.subtitle: The Cauldron of Awen, the Three Drops, the Flight of Shapes
domains.lead: Ceridwen is the keeper of the cauldron of awen — the poetic inspiration of Welsh tradition. From her house by Llyn Tegid she brews a year and a day for the three drops of inspired knowledge, hunts the servant-boy who steals them through every shape in creation, swallows him as a grain of wheat, and gives him back to the world as Taliesin, the greatest poet Wales remembers. The early Welsh sources concur on the essential fact: she is the owner of the cauldron that is the source of poetic inspiration.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Awen
cards.desc: Boiled a year and a day from the books of the feryllt, the alchemist's art, until three drops of inspired knowledge should rise from it.

cards.name: The Three Drops
cards.desc: All the virtue of the brew gathered in three drops — meant for her ugly son, splashed instead on the finger of Gwion Bach, who put it to his lips.

cards.name: The Flight of Shapes
cards.desc: Hare and greyhound, fish and otter, bird and hawk — the pursuit through every form until the grain of wheat meets the high-crested black hen.

cards.name: Llyn Tegid
cards.desc: The lake of Tegid Foel — modern Bala Lake, the largest natural lake in Wales — beside which her household stood and which still keeps her husband's name.

symbols.name: The cauldron
symbols.meaning: Inspiration brewed by art and patience — knowledge as something cooked, not granted

symbols.name: The three drops
symbols.meaning: The whole of awen compressed into an accident — inspiration that chooses its own vessel

symbols.name: The high-crested black hen
symbols.meaning: The final shape of the hunt: the swallowing that is not death but the first cell of a poet

symbols.name: The hide bag
symbols.meaning: The coracle-skin sewn round the unwanted child and given to the sea — rejection that becomes deliverance

symbols.name: The weir on the Dyfi
symbols.meaning: Gwyddno's salmon-weir where the bag comes to rest — the threshold between the hunted boy and the radiant brow

symbols.name: Llyn Tegid
symbols.meaning: The lake that still bears her husband's name — the story's anchor in real Welsh geography

mythology.lead: Ceridwen's whole dossier is a single tale — Hanes Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin — preserved in sixteenth-century Welsh manuscripts and customarily printed with the Mabinogion, though it is none of the Four Branches. Within that tale she owns its great engine: the cauldron, the hunt, and the rebirth.

myths.title: The Household by Llyn Tegid
myths.text: In the beginning, the tale says, Ceridwen lived beside Llyn Tegid in the land of Penllyn, the wife of Tegid Foel — Tegid the Bald — whose name the lake still carries. They had two children whose fortunes were weighed in opposite scales: a daughter, Creirwy, the fairest maiden in the world, and a son, Morfran, so dark and ill-favoured that he was called Afagddu, Utter Darkness. No god could have made the boy handsome; but Ceridwen was skilled in the arts, and she resolved to give him what nature had refused — knowledge and the gift of poetry, so that his birth might yet be honoured among men of culture.

myths.title: The Cauldron of a Year and a Day
myths.text: From the books of the feryllt — the Welsh name for the alchemist's art — Ceridwen compounded a cauldron of Inspiration and Science. It must boil a year and a day, ceaselessly, until three drops of the spirit of inspiration should be won from it. To keep the vigil she set a blind man, Morda, to kindle the fire beneath, and a servant-boy, Gwion Bach, son of Gwreang of Llanfair in Powys, to stir the pot. The design was exact and the patience enormous: everything in the tale that follows is the unmaking of this design by a single splash.

myths.title: The Three Drops and the Flight of Shapes
myths.text: At the year's end the three charmed drops leapt from the cauldron — and fell, not on Morfran, but on the finger of Gwion Bach. The boy put his burning finger in his mouth, and in that instant all the awen was his: he knew all that was past and all that was to come, and knew above all that Ceridwen would kill him. He fled. She pursued; and the pursuit is the oldest Welsh telling of the magic flight, the transformation chase of the folktales. He became a hare; she became a greyhound and gained on him. He leapt into a river and became a fish; she became an otter-bitch behind him. He rose into the air as a bird; she was a hawk on his wing. Every shape he took, she took its hunter.

myths.title: The Grain of Wheat and the Black Hen
myths.text: Spent at last, Gwion dropped into a barn and hid himself as one grain of winnowed wheat on the threshing-floor. Ceridwen became a high-crested black hen, went to the wheat, found the grain, and swallowed it. The swallowing is the tale's hinge: she carried him nine months, and when she bore him again he was so beautiful that she could not do what she had sworn — she could not kill him. So she sewed him in a hide bag and cast him into the sea, to the mercy of God, on the twenty-ninth of April. With that, Ceridwen passes out of her own story; she never appears again.

myths.title: The Radiant Brow
myths.text: The sea carried the bag to the salmon-weir of Gwyddno Garanhir, near the mouth of the Dyfi, and there on May Day Gwyddno's son Elffin found it among the fish. Opening it, he saw the boy's forehead and cried out what became a name: 'Behold the radiant brow' — tal iesin. 'Taliesin be I called,' the child answered, and as Elffin carried him home on horseback the boy sang his first poem, a song of consolation: Fair Elphin, cease your weeping. Years later, when Maelgwn Gwynedd imprisoned Elffin, the boy Taliesin went to the king's court, shamed every bard in the hall with poems they could not match, foretold the king's death, and freed his foster-father. The inspiration Ceridwen brewed for one son had become the making of another: the greatest poet of the Welsh tradition is, in the end, her child — swallowed, carried, born again, and set adrift by her own hands.

lore.syncretism: The strongest cross-border parallels are Irish. The accidental acquisition of a wisdom brewed for another is the plot of the Irish boyhood deeds of Finn mac Cumaill: cooking the salmon of knowledge for his master Finnéces, the boy Finn burns his thumb, puts it in his mouth, and the knowledge intended for the teacher passes to the servant — the same economy of the three drops and the burning finger. The swallowing that becomes rebirth has its Irish twin in Tochmarc Étaíne, where Étaín, transformed into a fly, falls into a cup of wine, is swallowed by the wife of Étar, and is born again into the mortal world. And the cauldron itself is pan-Celtic furniture: [[dagda|the Dagda]]'s cauldron from Murias feeds every company that comes to it, while the Old Irish text The Cauldron of Poesy locates a cauldron of poetry inside every human being. Folklorists — Juliette Wood chief among them — have shown that Hanes Taliesin braids these native strands with international folktale types, above all the magic flight with its transformation chase. The last syncretism is modern: Iolo Morganwg's Barddas set Ceridwen and the awen at the centre of revival Druidry, and modern Druids and pagans honour her as goddess of the cauldron — a reception Ronald Hutton's histories of the revival document and dissect.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest carried the Tale of Taliesin into English in the nineteenth century, appended to her Mabinogion, and the witch of Llyn Tegid entered the English-speaking imagination beside the Four Branches she never belonged to. Patrick K. Ford's edition and translation fixed the tale's modern scholarly form. Robert Graves made her a figure of international consequence: The White Goddess (1948) read Ceridwen's cauldron and her hunt as the grammar of all true poetry, and though Celticists have never accepted Graves's method, his book set her at the centre of twentieth-century writing about the muse. In Wales the awen she brewed never left the tradition — the word still names poetic inspiration at the National Eisteddfod, and modern Druid orders invoke it in her name — while modern paganism worldwide honours her as keeper of the cauldron of transformation. The name itself, rare in the medieval record, has come back into use as a Welsh given name, carried by the only myth in the language in which a goddess's failure becomes a nation's poetry.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ceridwen is the only great figure of Welsh tradition whose myth is a failure, and whose failure is a gift. She plans everything: the books consulted, the fire kept, the boy set to stir, the year counted to its day. And the plan is perfect except for the one thing no plan commands — where the drops fall. The inspiration she cooked for the son she pitied goes to the son she hunts, and everything she does to recover it only completes the gift: the chase teaches him every shape in creation, the swallowing carries him through the longest transformation of all, and the bag she sews to drown him is the coracle that brings him to his name.

That is the deepest thing the Welsh tradition knows about poetry: it cannot be inherited by arrangement. It is brewed in patience and received by accident; it belongs to whoever is standing by the pot with a burning finger. Ceridwen loses the awen and gains the poet — and the tale does not call her defeated. It simply follows the boy to the sea, and lets the witch of Llyn Tegid rest, her cauldron empty, her work done, her name over the door of every song that comes unplanned.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Ceridwen — the tale that contains her, Hanes Taliesin, survives in sixteenth-century manuscripts, above all the chronicle of Elis Gruffydd (NLW MS 5276D, c. 1550) and the copy of John Jones of Gellilyfdy (c. 1607), while earlier Welsh poetry attests the name in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven. Middle and Modern Welsh write the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: ceridwen.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/ceridwen/ in the meantime.

lore.archaeology: Ceridwen is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and pre-Christian Wales left no theonymic epigraphy of the continental kind. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The fullest early text of Hanes Taliesin is embedded in the great world-chronicle of Elis Gruffydd, a Welsh soldier and chronicler, compiled c. 1530–1552 (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, MS 5276D); a second version was copied by the recusant scribe John Jones of Gellilyfdy around 1607. The name itself is older than its tale: medieval Welsh poetry preserves it in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven, and the triads' editors record that the early sources agree on her one fixed attribute — the cauldron of awen. The geography of the story is real and still legible: Llyn Tegid, her lake, is Bala Lake in Gwynedd, the largest natural lake in Wales, which keeps her husband Tegid Foel's name; and Gwyddno's weir, where the bag comes ashore, stands in the tradition at the Dyfi estuary below his drowned realm. No sanctuary of hers is known, and none is claimed: her monument is the tale itself, and the lake that still carries the name.
